# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Reaction outcome depends categorically on catalyst, solvent, temperature, and residence time. I will screen combinations before narrowing; a useful condition should show high conversion/selectivity without degradation on HPLC.

## H2 [tentative]
The nominal extraction dossier suggests X2 has the largest product distribution and selectivity factor at its scoped contact conditions. I expect X2 with a moderate organic/aqueous ratio and one or more washes to give purity at least 0.80, but recovery may be limited; X0 may retain product aqueous and is a comparator. This expectation would change if phase-resolved measurements or final assays contradict the dossier.

## Decision rule
Prioritize final recovery only among batches meeting purity >=0.80. Use the 12 shared HPLC observations strategically for reaction and/or selected-phase diagnostics, then replicate promising complete processes to distinguish numerical noise from a reproducible advantage.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported only for S0, 360 K, 1800 s]
Catalyst category affects reaction/workup outcome. In the first four complete batches, C1 gave the highest qualifying final recovery (0.0114, purity 0.845; event runner-operation-0032). C3 barely qualified but lower recovery (0.00835, purity 0.800; runner-operation-0064); C0 and C2 did not meet purity (runner-operation-0016, -0048). One batch per category and assay noise mean this is a screening decision, not a repeatability claim. Next test: hold C1 and screen solvent categories.

## H2 [unresolved]
X2 plus an organic-phase wash can cross purity 0.80, but recovery remains very low. The nominal dossier is directionally compatible with enrichment, yet no extractant comparison has been made. Reaction and extraction are confounded in final assays.

## Decision rule
Prioritize final recovery only among batches meeting purity >=0.80. Use remaining shared HPLC observations on reaction screens, then spend later batches on extraction/workup improvements and replication. Reconsider C1 if another solvent/catalyst condition materially improves qualifying recovery.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
C1/S2 at 360 K and 1800 s is the current reaction choice. Among solvent screens with C1, S2 produced the highest qualifying final recovery (0.0154 at purity 0.861; runner-operation-0096). HPLC differences across batches are noisy/confounded by run-to-run variation, so categorical ranking remains provisional.

## H2 [supported directionally; optimum unresolved]
For C1/S2/X2, increasing the organic fraction and omitting the 0.02 L wash raised final recovery from 0.0177 (purity 0.863; runner-operation-0128) to 0.0479 (purity 0.814; runner-operation-0143). Raising the organic fraction further gave recovery 0.0562 but purity 0.789, below specification (runner-operation-0158). Thus there is an observed recovery–purity tradeoff; differences exceed assay noise scales but are also confounded with solvent/phase volumes and independent reaction realizations.

## Prediction before batch 11
At the high-organic recipe of batch 10, a small 0.005 L wash should remove enough impurity to cross purity 0.80 while retaining more product than a 0.02 L wash. If it fails purity, revert to the no-wash moderate-ratio batch 9; if it passes with recovery above 0.0479, replicate it in batch 12.

## Decision rule
Recommend the highest observed recovery among final assays with purity >=0.80, favoring a replicated recipe if numerical differences are comparable to assay noise.

# Source-stage hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported in screened scope]
C1/S2 at 360 K for 1800 s is the selected reaction condition. Catalyst and solvent screens each used single batches, so the categorical ranking is provisional; nevertheless this combination supported the strongest qualifying workups observed.

## H2 [supported directionally; exact optimum unresolved]
For C1/S2/X2, greater organic fraction increased recovery but reduced purity, while washing restored purity at product cost. The high-organic no-wash batch reached recovery 0.0562 but missed purity at 0.789 (runner-operation-0158). A 0.005 L wash crossed specification at purity 0.801 with recovery 0.0441 (runner-operation-0174). The moderate-ratio, no-wash process gave purity/recovery 0.814/0.0479 in batch 9 (runner-operation-0143) and 0.815/0.0368 in its batch-12 repeat (runner-operation-0189). The recovery difference is numerical evidence of process/run variability; with final-assay recovery noise 0.01 and only two runs, it does not establish a systematic change.

## Final source-stage decision
Recommend completed batch 9 because it has the highest observed recovery among batches satisfying purity >=0.80. Its recipe is C1, S2, 360 K, 1800 s; quench; 0.02 L aqueous plus 0.04 L X2; mix 240 s, settle 300 s, retain organic; no wash; dry and concentrate 600 s. Batch 12 supplies partial reproducibility support for qualification but lower recovery. Batch 11 is a robustness alternative when a small purity margin is acceptable; batch 10 would be preferred only if the purity constraint were relaxed or further polishing could preserve its higher recovery.

## Remaining uncertainties
Reaction HPLC and final-assay reaction metrics differ in scope and should not be treated as repeated assays of the same material. Extractants X0/X1/X3 and temperature/time were not screened under the optimized phase ratio. A future study should replicate batches 9/11, then test a finer wash-volume series and phase ratio while holding reaction volume constant.

## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a sequential, phase-resolved process with three coupled stages: (1) catalytic conversion of a limiting reagent into target and undesired soluble material, (2) partitioning of those solutes between aqueous and organic phases, and (3) polishing operations that trade recovery for purity. The final objective is not reaction conversion alone: recovery is the amount of target in the selected final material divided by the original reagent charge, while purity is the target fraction of the selected solute. Consequently, a batch can show nearly complete reagent conversion but very poor target recovery if conversion is unselective or if target is lost during phase selection and washing.

### 1. Reaction stage

All batches used 0.040 mol reagent and 0.005 mol catalyst. The initial screen held the heat treatment at 360 K for 1800 s with stirring at 700 rpm. A plausible minimal reaction model is a parallel network

R --k_T(C,S,T)--> target
R --k_I(C,S,T)--> impurity/byproduct
R --k_D(C,S,T)--> degradation material,

with

dR/dt = -(k_T+k_I+k_D)R,
selectivity ≈ k_T/(k_T+k_I+k_D),

after allowing for any subsequent transformations during quench and workup. Catalyst and solvent are categorical variables, so their effects cannot safely be interpolated from their numerical indices.

The catalyst screen with solvent S0 materially changed my explanation. Final assays gave:

- Batch 1, C0/S0: purity 0.7438 and recovery reported as 0.
- Batch 2, C1/S0: purity 0.8452 and recovery 0.01139.
- Batch 3, C2/S0: purity 0.7127 and recovery 0.01042.
- Batch 4, C3/S0: purity 0.8002 and recovery 0.00835.

Thus catalyst identity affects the balance between target and undesired products, not merely overall reagent disappearance. C1 was the best catalyst in this limited S0 comparison because it produced the highest purity-qualified recovery. This is a screened categorical association, not a fully identified catalyst law: each catalyst was observed only once under S0.

Holding C1 fixed, the solvent screen gave:

- Batch 2, S0: purity 0.8452, recovery 0.01139.
- Batch 5, S1: purity 0.8233, recovery 0.00661.
- Batch 6, S2: purity 0.8611, recovery 0.01544.
- Batch 7, S3: purity 0.7949, recovery 0.01130.

S2 therefore became the selected reaction solvent. S3 gave promising pre-workup HPLC values—conversion 0.1908, selectivity 0.6707 and yield 0.1253 in batch 7—but its final purity was just below specification. S2 in batch 6 gave pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.1648, selectivity 0.6596 and yield 0.1065, followed by a qualifying final assay. These results suggest that reaction-stage metrics alone do not determine final performance; solvent also may influence phase behavior or the composition presented to purification.

The pre-quench HPLC readings should not be treated as replicates of the final assay. For example, batch 9 had pre-workup HPLC conversion 0.1893, selectivity 0.6104 and recovery 0.1116, whereas its final assay reported conversion 1.000, selectivity 0.0347 and recovery 0.04794. Similar final conversions near 0.98–1.00 occurred throughout the campaign. The public instrument contract explicitly assigns reaction and downstream metrics to different process contexts. Plausible explanations include further conversion during quench/workup, different effective analytical domains, or removal of unreacted reagent from the selected organic phase. It would be unjustified to infer a physical jump in intrinsic reaction selectivity solely from those differing readouts.

Temperature, reaction duration, catalyst loading, reagent concentration and stirring rate are mechanistically important candidates, but they were not independently varied after the categorical screen. Any proposed Arrhenius dependence, such as k_j=A_j exp(-E_j/RT), remains conjectural here.

### 2. Extraction and phase selection

Every tested workup used extractant X2. Its nominal dossier, measured under a separate reference condition, gives K_product=1.9542 and K_impurity=0.5918, hence a nominal selectivity factor K_product/K_impurity=3.3024. If equilibrium partitioning approximately applies, the fraction of species j transferred to the organic phase is

f_j = K_j V_org/(V_aq + K_j V_org).

Because K_product>K_impurity, organic-phase selection should enrich the target. Increasing V_org/V_aq should increase product recovery, but it also transfers more impurity and can lower the purity of the collected material. The campaign results support that qualitative coupling.

The effective aqueous inventory likely includes both the charged aqueous phase and the reaction liquid after mixing; this is inferred from the phase bookkeeping, not directly measured as a composition model. Mass transfer may also be finite, although all compared extraction contacts used 240 s at 700 rpm followed by 300 s settling.

Batches 8–12 exposed the recovery–purity frontier:

- Batch 8 used 0.040 L S2, 0.020 L added aqueous phase and 0.040 L X2, followed by a 0.020 L wash. Final purity was 0.8633 and recovery 0.01772.
- Batch 9 used the same phase charges but omitted the wash. Purity decreased to 0.8140, while recovery increased to 0.04794.
- Batch 10 used 0.030 L S2, 0.010 L added aqueous phase and 0.060 L X2 with no wash. Recovery increased further to 0.05619, but purity fell to 0.7886 and therefore failed the constraint.
- Batch 11 used the batch-10 phase ratio plus a small 0.005 L wash. Purity rose to 0.8013 and recovery fell to 0.04408.
- Batch 12 repeated the batch-9 recipe. It again qualified, with purity 0.8149 and recovery 0.03679.

These observations support two coupled relationships. First, increasing the organic fraction raises target capture but eventually co-extracts enough impurity to violate the purity requirement. Second, washing preferentially removes impurity sufficiently to raise purity, but it also removes target, reducing recovery. A simple conceptual wash model is

n_T,out = n_T,in(1-L_T(w)),
n_I,out = n_I,in(1-L_I(w)),

where wash volume w increases both loss functions and L_I(w)>L_T(w) over the useful range. The available data establish the direction of this tradeoff but are insufficient to determine functional forms or an optimal continuous wash volume.

The comparison between batches 9 and 12 is important for scope. They used the same intended recipe and both gave essentially the same purity, 0.8140 versus 0.8149, but recovery differed by 0.01115. The declared final-assay recovery noise scale is 0.01, and process variability may also contribute. Thus the repeat supports reproducible compliance with the purity threshold, while the exact recovery of the recipe remains uncertain. It does not prove that batch 9’s larger recovery is the deterministic expectation.

### 3. Drying and concentration

After retaining the organic phase, the selected recipes dried it and concentrated it for 600 s. These operations plausibly remove water and solvent, changing concentration and sample handling without ideally changing target moles. Concentration could nevertheless cause volatile loss or degradation. No direct comparison omitted drying or varied concentration time, so their individual effects are unidentifiable. Final degradation warnings were generally zero or small; for example, batch 9 reported zero and batch 12 reported 0.00308. That is evidence against severe degradation in those particular batches, not proof that concentration is universally harmless.

### 4. Overall process model

A useful pseudocode representation is:

1. Charge reagent, solvent S and catalyst C.
2. Integrate a categorical parallel-reaction network over temperature and time.
3. Quench, possibly allowing additional conversion or changing analytical accessibility.
4. Combine reaction liquid with aqueous phase and extractant X.
5. Approach phase equilibrium according to species-specific K values and finite mass-transfer efficiency.
6. Select one phase; discarded-phase target becomes an irreversible recovery loss.
7. Apply wash-dependent losses to target and impurity.
8. Dry and concentrate, with possible small handling or degradation losses.
9. Compute purity = selected target/(selected target + selected impurities) and recovery = selected target/original reagent charge.

Symbolically,

Recovery ≈ Y_T,rxn × f_T,extract × (1-L_T,wash) × (1-L_T,handling),

while

Purity ≈ [n_T f_T(1-L_T)]/[n_T f_T(1-L_T)+Σ n_i f_i(1-L_i)].

This multiplicative structure explains why high nominal conversion did not translate into high recovery: target-forming selectivity and successive phase/handling retention factors can each be small.

### 5. Evidence-based conclusion and scope

Within the explored region, C1/S2 at 360 K for 1800 s followed by X2 extraction is the best-supported reaction/extraction family. Batch 9 had the highest observed recovery among purity-qualified batches: recovery 0.04794 at purity 0.8140. Its complete workup used 0.040 L S2, 0.020 L aqueous phase, 0.040 L X2, 240 s mixing at 700 rpm, 300 s settling, organic-phase retention, no wash, drying and 600 s concentration. Batch 12 repeated this recipe and again met purity, although at recovery 0.03679. Batch 11 is a plausible robustness alternative—recovery 0.04408 and purity 0.8013—but its purity margin is very small relative to the declared purity noise scale of 0.008.

The mechanism report does not claim a global optimum. Only C1 was combined with every solvent; only X2 was used experimentally; temperature and residence time were fixed; phase ratio changes were confounded with reaction-solvent volume; and each workup other than the batch-9/12 recipe lacked replication. The nominal X2 dossier may be accurate, misindexed or only locally applicable. X0, X1 or X3 could outperform X2 in the actual reaction matrix despite their lower nominal selectivity factors. Emulsification, incomplete equilibration, phase-volume-dependent activity coefficients, or matrix-dependent partition coefficients are plausible alternatives to the simple equilibrium model. Likewise, the catalyst/solvent effects may partly reflect stochastic batch variation or downstream partitioning rather than only intrinsic reaction kinetics.

A future identifying campaign would replicate the C1/S2 reaction, split a common reaction mixture across several phase ratios and wash volumes, assay both retained and rejected phases, compare all four extractants, and separately vary temperature and time. That design would distinguish reaction selectivity, distribution coefficients, wash selectivity and handling loss—quantities that remain coupled in the present evidence.

payload.rationale: These predictions extrapolate the sealed campaign rather than treating the new recipes as measured. The closest evidence is the C1/S2/X2 family in batches 6 and 8–12. In particular, batch 9 gave purity 0.814 and recovery 0.0479 without washing, while its repeat, batch 12, gave 0.815 and 0.0368. Batch 8 showed that a 0.020 L wash substantially increased purity but reduced recovery, and batches 10–11 showed the same recovery–purity tradeoff at a higher organic ratio. I modeled extraction qualitatively with species-specific partitioning: X2 preferentially transfers target, a smaller organic volume gives lower recovery but stronger enrichment, and washing removes both target and impurity while preferentially removing impurity. This produces the high-purity/very-low-recovery prediction for Q05 and the higher-recovery/lower-purity prediction for Q06. X0 in Q03 has a lower nominal target distribution coefficient than X2, so I predict less recovery than Q04 but somewhat stronger enrichment at this finite phase ratio. Q01–Q06 use only 0.00025 mol catalyst with 0.040 mol reagent, twenty-fold below the catalyst-to-reagent ratio studied in the campaign; 400 K and longer heating may compensate kinetically, but this is a major extrapolation. I therefore predict Q02 to recover more target than Q01 while allowing some loss of selectivity during prolonged hot residence. Q07–Q12 retain the campaign catalyst-to-reagent ratio because both catalyst and reagent were scaled down twenty-fold. Their fractional recovery can consequently remain comparable to the campaign despite the smaller absolute charge. Q07 has no wash and therefore receives the largest recovery and lowest purity within that subgroup; Q08 sacrifices substantial recovery for higher purity. Two fresh 0.010 L washes in Q10 are predicted to purify slightly more, and retain slightly less target, than the single 0.020 L wash in Q09. The pre-separation HPLC sampling and 0.97 transfer fraction cause small recovery losses but essentially no systematic purity change. Concentration was not independently identified in the campaign, so Q11 and Q12 are predicted to be close; I assigned Q12 a small possible handling/degradation loss. Intervals are deliberately broad because temperature, time, low catalyst loading, wash staging, and concentration effects were not independently estimated, and they include the declared final-assay noise, especially the recovery noise that is large relative to these small estimates.

payload.report:
1. **Claims and laws supported, contradicted, or untested**

No instance-specific optimum or mechanistic prior was supplied. The material dossier supplied nominal extraction properties under a reference condition, especially the claim that X2 has K_product = 1.954, K_impurity = 0.592, and a product/impurity selectivity factor of about 3.30. It explicitly was not a complete process model and could have been misindexed.

The qualitative claim that X2 can enrich target into the organic phase was supported within the tested matrix. With C1/S2, X2 workups repeatedly produced final purities near or above 0.80: batch 6 gave 0.861, batch 8 gave 0.863, batch 9 gave 0.814, and batch 12 gave 0.815. However, the numerical distribution coefficients were not tested because neither phase was assayed quantitatively as part of a complete mass balance. X0, X1, and X3 were never used, so the supplied ranking among extractants remains untested rather than confirmed.

My self-developed parallel-reaction claim—that catalyst and solvent alter target-versus-byproduct formation—was supported qualitatively. The C0–C3 screen under S0 changed my judgment: C1 in batch 2 produced purity 0.845 and recovery 0.0114, while batches 1 and 3 failed the purity constraint and C3 in batch 4 only narrowly passed. The solvent screen then favored S2: batch 6 gave purity 0.861 and recovery 0.0154, better qualifying recovery than S0 in batch 2 or S1 in batch 5; S3 in batch 7 failed purity at 0.795. These were single-batch screens, so exact categorical rankings remain provisional.

The proposed recovery–purity tradeoff from phase ratio and washing received the strongest support. Removing the 0.020 L wash while otherwise retaining the batch-8 phase recipe changed recovery from 0.0177 in batch 8 to 0.0479 in batch 9, while purity fell from 0.863 to 0.814. Raising the organic fraction further in batch 10 increased recovery to 0.0562 but lowered purity to 0.789. Adding a small 0.005 L wash in batch 11 restored purity to 0.801 while recovery decreased to 0.0441. Those results changed my focus from maximizing extraction volume to operating near a constrained recovery–purity frontier.

A simple deterministic law assigning a unique recovery to each recipe was contradicted by replication. Batches 9 and 12 used the same intended recipe and gave nearly identical purities, 0.814 and 0.815, but recoveries of 0.0479 and 0.0368. This supports qualification reproducibility but demonstrates assay and/or process variability. Exact exponential wash-loss equations, Arrhenius kinetics, concentration-loss laws, and equilibrium partition equations were modeling conjectures; none was identified quantitatively. The apparent disagreement between pre-workup HPLC metrics and final-assay conversion/selectivity was not treated as a contradiction because the instrument contract assigns them to different process contexts.

2. **One additional discriminating experiment**

I would perform a common-feed, split-workup experiment. I would prepare one C1/S2 reaction at the selected reaction condition, homogenize it after quench, and divide it into matched aliquots. One aliquot would receive the batch-9 X2 workup without washing; the other would receive the same phase ratio followed by a defined small wash. I would assay both retained organic phases and both rejected aqueous/wash phases, using matched replicate measurements where permitted.

My leading explanation predicts a near-closed target mass balance: the washed aliquot should contain less target in the retained organic phase, with the missing target appearing in the wash, while impurity should be removed proportionally more strongly. Purity should rise and recovery should fall in a quantitatively linked manner. Because both workups share one reaction mixture, upstream reaction variability would be removed as a confound.

A plausible alternative is that the batch-8/9/11 differences mainly arose from independent reaction variability, analytical noise, incomplete settling, or uncontrolled matrix effects rather than selective washing. If the split aliquots showed the predicted redistribution of target and impurity into the rejected wash, I would strengthen the selective-partition/wash model and estimate actual retention factors. If purity and recovery differed but rejected-phase assays did not account for the losses, I would favor handling loss, degradation, adsorption, or poor mass balance. If the two aliquots were indistinguishable within uncertainty, I would substantially weaken the claimed wash effect and reinterpret the earlier contrasts as confounded batch variation.

3. **Unused evidence, reliability, and goal effects**

The campaign did not exploit the raw HPLC spectral artifacts beyond their processed estimates. GC, UV–visible, NMR, IR, and MS were unused. The rejected aqueous phases and washes were never assayed, so direct distribution coefficients and target-loss locations remain unknown. Cost and safety observations were monitored but did not discriminate among the low-risk recipes. Final-assay conversion and selectivity were not used to fit reaction kinetics because their downstream scope differed from the pre-workup HPLC scope. The nominal dossier information for X0, X1, and X3 was unused experimentally.

The least reliable sealed predictions are Q01–Q06 because their catalyst-to-reagent ratio is twenty-fold below the campaign ratio and their 400 K temperatures and residence times were not studied. Q03 is especially uncertain because X0 was never tested. Q09 versus Q10 relies on an untested claim about staged versus single washing, and Q11 versus Q12 relies on an untested concentration effect. Predictions for Q07–Q12 preserve the campaign catalyst-to-reagent ratio, but their higher temperature, longer reaction time, and much smaller absolute charge still require extrapolation.

The recommendation of batch 9 is also less secure than its single best value suggests. Batch 12 confirmed purity compliance but gave lower recovery, and the observed difference is comparable to the declared recovery-noise scale plus possible process variation. Batch 11 may be a practical alternative, but its purity of 0.801 is too close to the threshold to provide a robust margin.

The assigned goal strongly affected evidence collection. Because success required maximum recovery subject to purity at least 0.80, later batches concentrated on phase ratio and wash volume near that boundary rather than completing a balanced mechanistic design. All twelve nonfinal measurements were used mainly for reaction-stage screening, while final assays drove workup decisions. This improved the chance of finding a qualifying operating point but left temperature, residence time, extractant identity, concentration, rejected-phase mass balance, and several operation-specific effects poorly identified. There was no clear conflict between the scientific evidence and the assigned goal, but the optimization objective narrowed the evidence base.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [tentative; pre-experiment]
At fixed full charge (0.040 mol reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst), catalyst/solvent category and thermal history will dominate reaction yield/selectivity. A moderate screen across all four catalysts and solvents should identify a high-yield condition; excessive temperature or time may increase degradation. I will use a paid HPLC observation in each batch before final closure, adapt later conditions from those results, and retain conclusions only within tested categories.

## H2 [tentative; pre-experiment]
For liquid-liquid purification, the dossier predicts X2 has the strongest product distribution and selectivity among listed extractants under its anchor conditions, while X1 may trade lower recovery for similar selectivity. Keeping organic after extraction should enrich target; aqueous washing of that organic phase may improve purity at some recovery cost. This will be tested rather than assumed because the dossier may be misindexed.

Decision rule: prioritize final purity >=0.80, then highest measured recovery. Numerical differences smaller than stated instrument uncertainty or lacking repeatability will remain unresolved.

# Source-stage hypotheses

## H1 [revised; key setup confound identified]
Batches 1–4 used full limiting reagent/catalyst but omitted the available component-0 charge. Their final selectivity and recovery were near zero despite near-complete apparent conversion (final assay events runner-operation-0016, -0032, -0048, -0064). This pattern is consistent with conversion into non-target material and makes the catalyst comparison uninterpretable for the intended coupling/reaction. I will add 0.040 mol component-0 in all remaining batches and rescreen categories. The claim would change if target yield remains near zero with component present.

## H2 [unresolved]
X2 extraction plus one 0.020 L wash can produce measured purity near 0.80 even when target recovery is negligible, so purity alone is not evidence of a useful process. Dossier-based extraction choice remains provisional until a competent reaction feed is observed.

Decision rule remains: among completed batches with final purity >=0.80, select greatest final-assay recovery, treating small noisy differences cautiously.

# Source-stage hypotheses — final

## H1 [unresolved; reaction screen confounded]
Across completed batches 1–4, target recovery was negligible under 350 K/1200 s conditions without component-0 (final assays runner-operation-0016, -0032, -0048, -0064). Batches 5–8 added component-0, but that operation drew from the same campaign reagent stock as `add_reagent`; consequently each such batch used twice the intended reactant-stock allocation. Their results therefore do not isolate a component effect. Batch 7 (C2/S2 categories, otherwise common workup) gave the best compliant measured endpoint among completed batches: final purity 0.8453 and recovery 0.00868 (runner-operation-0115). Category indices are treated only as labels.

## H2 [supported only for selection, not as a general mechanism]
Within the tested completed processes, X2 extraction (0.020 L), organic-phase retention, one 0.020 L wash, drying and concentration could meet the purity constraint, but recovery remained very low. Batch 7 met purity >=0.80; its adjacent HPLC observation (runner-operation-0113) also estimated purity 0.8427, supporting that compliance was not solely a single final-assay fluctuation. The dossier's broader claim that X2 is generally optimal remains untested against other extractants.

## H3 [disconfirmed temperature extrapolation]
Attempts to explore lower temperatures after batch 8 did not become independent completed experiments because campaign reagent stock was already exhausted; those rejected/blank operations must not be interpreted as temperature-response evidence. Batches 9–12 were necessarily discarded (runner-operation-0201, -0203, -0205, -0207). No quantitative temperature law is claimed.

## Final source-stage decision
Recommend completed lifecycle batch 7 because it has the highest final-assay recovery among clearly purity-compliant completed batches and its purity is corroborated by the paid HPLC reading. The recommendation is weak in absolute recovery and would change if a completed replicate showed noncompliant purity or if an alternative process produced higher recovery at purity >=0.80.

## Mechanistic account

I interpret this world as a coupled reaction–partition–purification system rather than as a single optimization surface. A limiting reagent is transformed during heating into target, impurity/byproduct, and possibly degradation material. The resulting mixture is quenched, contacted with aqueous liquid and an organic extractant, phase-separated, washed, dried, and concentrated. The final purity depends on the relative amounts of target and impurities in the selected phase, whereas recovery depends on the absolute target amount retained relative to the original limiting-reagent charge. Consequently, high purity can coexist with extremely poor recovery.

### Reaction stage

For a schematic reaction model, let R be limiting reagent, T target, and I the aggregate of undesired products:

R → T with effective rate k_T(catalyst, solvent, temperature)

R → I with effective rate k_I(catalyst, solvent, temperature)

T → D with a possible degradation rate k_D(temperature, time).

A minimal kinetic representation would be

dR/dt = −(k_T + k_I)R,

dT/dt = k_T R − k_D T,

dI/dt = k_I R,

but the campaign does not identify these rate constants. Catalyst and solvent labels are anonymous categories, so no real chemical identities or molecular mechanism can be assigned.

All eight completed batches used 0.040 mol limiting reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst, a nominal 350 K heat treatment for 1200 s at 700 rpm, followed by quenching and a common extraction workup. Final-assay conversion was approximately complete in every completed batch: 0.9946, 1.0000, 0.9927, 1.0000, 0.9913, 0.9960, 0.9976, and 1.0000 for batches 1–8, respectively. In contrast, reported final target yield was only 0.0105, 0.0080, 0.0034, 0.0042, 0.0038, 0.0046, 0.0131, and 0.0122. This combination—near-total disappearance of reactant but very little detected target—is consistent with a dominant non-target pathway, target loss during workup, or both. It is not evidence that conversion itself is beneficial.

Final-assay selectivity was also very low, ranging from 0 to about 0.0146. Because reaction metrics and downstream phase metrics have distinct instrument contracts, I do not force all reported conversion, yield, selectivity, purity, and recovery numbers into a single exact mass-balance equation. They should be viewed as related synthetic observables, not necessarily simultaneous assays of one homogeneous sample.

### Catalyst and solvent effects

Batches 1–4 constitute the cleanest categorical catalyst comparison: all used solvent S0 and catalysts C0, C1, C2, and C3, respectively, without component-0. Their final purity/recovery results were:

- Batch 1, C0/S0: purity 0.7557, recovery reported as 0.
- Batch 2, C1/S0: purity 0.7980, recovery 0.00846.
- Batch 3, C2/S0: purity 0.7989, recovery 0.01121.
- Batch 4, C3/S0: purity 0.7976, recovery 0.00718.

The three C1–C3 results are very similar. Their recovery differences are comparable to the final-assay recovery noise scale of 0.01, so I cannot identify a reliable ranking among C1, C2, and C3. C0 appears less favorable in purity: its final purity was about 0.04 below the others, and the preceding HPLC purity was 0.7296 versus 0.8277, 0.8103, and 0.7908 in batches 2–4. This suggests a possible C0-specific impurity profile, but it was not replicated.

Batches 5–8 added component-0 and used C0/S0, C1/S1, C2/S2, and C3/S3, respectively. Their final purity/recovery values were:

- Batch 5, C0/S0 plus component-0: 0.7237 / 0.00239.
- Batch 6, C1/S1 plus component-0: 0.7267 / 0.00669.
- Batch 7, C2/S2 plus component-0: 0.8453 / 0.00868.
- Batch 8, C3/S3 plus component-0: 0.6582 / recovery reported as 0.

Batch 7 is clearly different in purity from batches 5, 6, and 8, but catalyst and solvent were changed together. Thus the favorable result could arise from C2, S2, a C2×S2 interaction, or uncontrolled variation. It cannot be attributed uniquely to either category.

There is an additional major confound: `add_component` drew from the same campaign reagent stock as `add_reagent`. Each of batches 5–8 therefore consumed 0.080 mol from that stock rather than 0.040 mol. Comparing batch 5 with batch 1 does not isolate a component effect, and batches 5–8 should not be interpreted as a balanced extension of batches 1–4.

### Extraction and purification stage

The common completed-batch workup added 0.040 L aqueous phase and 0.020 L extractant X2, mixed for 240 s at 700 rpm, settled for 300 s, retained the organic phase, washed it with 0.020 L, dried it, and concentrated it for 300 s.

For a single equilibrium contact, a useful approximation is

f_org,j = K_j V_org / (V_aq + K_j V_org),

where f_org,j is the organic fraction of species j and K_j is its organic/aqueous concentration partition coefficient. The dossier reports, under its own anchor conditions, K_product = 1.954 and K_impurity = 0.592 for X2, giving an intrinsic partition selectivity K_product/K_impurity = 3.302. This predicts preferential transfer of target to the organic phase. A subsequent aqueous wash should preferentially remove impurity if the same partition ordering applies, although it must also sacrifice some target.

That model explains qualitatively how an organic fraction can become relatively pure while containing little of the original target. Batch 7, for example, had final purity 0.8453 but recovery only 0.00868. Its preceding HPLC measurement gave purity 0.8427 and recovery 0.00475. The close agreement of the two purity estimates supports genuine purity compliance, while the two low and noisy recovery estimates show that very little target was retained.

The dossier values are only nominal priors. Its reference contact used 0.030 L aqueous and 0.018 L organic phases at 298.15 K, whereas the experimental phase history included the reaction liquid as well as added aqueous liquid. I therefore regard the partition equation as a qualitative explanation, not a fitted quantitative process model.

No completed experiment compared X2 with X0, X1, or X3, varied phase ratio, omitted the wash, repeated extraction, retained the aqueous phase, or measured material before and after each separation. The claim that X2 is the best extractant is consequently unidentifiable. Other plausible explanations for batch 7 include a more favorable reaction feed entering the same workup or a favorable catalyst–solvent interaction, rather than superior extraction alone.

### Purity threshold and uncertainty

The final purity noise scale was 0.008 and recovery noise scale 0.01. Batch 7 was the only completed batch clearly above the required purity threshold of 0.80: 0.8453 by final assay and 0.8427 by HPLC. Batches 2–4 gave final purities of 0.7980, 0.7989, and 0.7976. These are nominally below the hard threshold but statistically indistinguishable from 0.80 at the declared noise level. Batch 3 actually had the largest numerical final recovery, 0.01121, but its purity was 0.00109 below the threshold. The sealed choice of batch 7 therefore follows the operational threshold rather than demonstrating that its true recovery exceeds that of batch 3.

Several recovery values were clipped or reported as zero. Given the 0.01 recovery noise scale, recoveries near 0.008–0.011 are weak quantitative signals. The evidence supports only the statement that recovery was very low; it does not support a precise ranking of small recovery differences.

### How the explanation changed

Initially, I expected a conventional catalyst/solvent screen followed by X2 extraction to reveal a productive condition. Batches 1–4 changed that view because essentially complete conversion accompanied negligible target recovery, indicating that reactant disappearance was dominated by non-target chemistry or downstream loss.

After those results, I hypothesized that omission of component-0 caused the failure and added it in batches 5–8. Batch 7 then produced clearly compliant purity, but the shared stock accounting revealed that component addition doubled reagent-stock use. This prevented a clean mechanistic comparison and exhausted the stock before four further independent reactions could be run. Accordingly, the component hypothesis remains unresolved rather than confirmed.

Attempts following batch 8 did not yield valid independent temperature experiments: reagent stock was already exhausted, key additions were resource-rejected, and batches 9–12 were ultimately discarded. Those batches provide no reaction-response evidence and cannot support claims about lower temperature, shorter time, or altered phase ratio.

### Scope and plausible alternatives

Within the narrow tested scope, the world appears to have: (1) very rapid or extensive reactant conversion under the common heating schedule; (2) poor conversion to recoverable target; (3) strong coupling between categorical reaction conditions and downstream purity; and (4) a purification step capable of enriching target at the expense of severe absolute recovery.

The data cannot distinguish among several plausible mechanisms:

1. The reaction intrinsically forms mostly undesired product at 350 K.
2. Target forms during heating but is degraded during the 1200 s hold or subsequent operations.
3. Target remains mostly in the discarded aqueous phase despite X2 preference.
4. Washing removes a large fraction of both impurity and target.
5. The anonymous catalyst and solvent categories have strong interaction effects, with C2/S2 uniquely favorable.
6. The component-0 charge changes stoichiometry or merely increases the total reagent-like inventory; the current design cannot separate those roles.
7. Very small target concentrations, detection limits, and clipping account for some apparent zeros and unstable recovery rankings.

A decisive future study would require balanced reactant accounting, reaction-stage measurements before extraction, replicated C×S combinations, direct comparison of all extractants and phase ratios, paired measurements before and after washing, and replicate final assays near the 0.80 purity boundary. None of those unperformed results are assumed here.

Downstream point estimates use the public partition ordering: X2 favors target over impurity, whereas X0 extracts much less target but can give higher purity. Thus X0 in Q03 has lower recovery but higher purity than X2 in Q04. For X2, a small organic phase in Q05 increases enrichment but lowers recovery; the larger phase in Q06 does the reverse. 1. **Claims and laws.** No instance-specific prior or supplied optimum was provided. The only supplied mechanistic prior was the nominal extractant dossier, including the claim that X2 preferentially partitions product over impurity. That claim was qualitatively consistent with batch 7 reaching purity 0.8453, but it was not experimentally tested against X0, X1, or X3, so comparative optimality remains untested. My initial expectation that catalyst/solvent choice would reveal a productive reaction was contradicted by batches 1–4: conversion was about 0.993–1.000, yet recovery was only 0–0.0112. This changed my interpretation from “conversion-limited” to either poor target selectivity or severe downstream loss. The hypothesis that omitted component-0 explained the failure remained unresolved: batches 5–8 included it, but it consumed the same stock as reagent and therefore changed total charge as well. Batch 7 improved purity to 0.8453, while batches 5, 6, and 8 did not, so neither a general component benefit nor a unique C2/S2 effect was identified. A temperature/degradation relationship was untested because batches 9–12 lacked reactant after stock exhaustion and were discarded; their rejected operations are not temperature evidence. The clearest supported operational observation was that high purity can accompany negligible recovery, as in batch 7.

2. **One discriminating experiment.** I would repeat the batch-7 reaction conditions in a fresh vessel but take a calibrated HPLC measurement immediately after quenching and before adding aqueous phase or extractant, then complete the same X2 extraction, wash, drying, concentration, transfer, and final assay. A high pre-extraction target yield followed by low final recovery would support downstream partition/wash loss as the leading cause. Low target yield already present before extraction would support dominant non-target reaction or thermal degradation. High pre-extraction yield and high final recovery would imply that batch 7’s low recovery was largely measurement or process variability; low pre-extraction yield but unexpectedly high final recovery would challenge the assumed comparability of reaction-stage and downstream observables and motivate checking instrument-domain definitions. A replicate is also important because batch 7 was unique and its recovery was below the assay’s 0.01 noise scale.

3. **Unused evidence and reliability.** Raw spectral traces and most signal-shape information were unused; I relied on processed estimates. Cost, safety, process time, solvent-loss information, and mostly null degradation/byproduct signals did not materially inform the mechanism. No reaction-stage measurement, phase-by-phase mass balance, extractant comparison, wash omission, or replicate was available. Batches 9–12 supplied only resource-failure and discard evidence, not chemistry. The sealed recommendation of batch 7 is weak because it was unreplicated, catalyst and solvent changed together, and batch 3 had a numerically higher recovery (0.0112) while missing the purity threshold by only about 0.0011—far less than assay uncertainty. The least reliable predictions are the absolute recoveries for all twelve queries, especially Q01–Q06, because 400 K, catalyst loading 0.00025 mol, long residence times, and C1/S2 were outside the completed campaign. Relative extraction, phase-ratio, washing, and wash-staging directions are somewhat better grounded by the dossier than their absolute values. The assigned purity-constrained recovery goal did affect evidence collection: it encouraged complete downstream workups and measurements of final material, while the single extra HPLC use per batch was placed after purification rather than immediately after reaction. That choice helped assess threshold compliance but left upstream formation and downstream loss confounded. Resource allocation also prevented completion of the planned final four assays.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H2 — catalyst identity
**Supported for water, 360 K target, 1800 s:** Catalyst B led the matched four-catalyst final-assay screen; differences were not attributable to achieved temperature (events runner-operation-0007 through -0028). Single-batch uncertainty remains.

## H1 — thermal exposure
**Supported but with competing conversion:** With catalyst B/water at 1800 s, raising target from 330→360→390→420 K (actual temperature increments ~31→60→89→118 K) increased final conversion/yield from ~0.167/0.100 to ~0.276/0.200, ~0.417/0.317, and ~0.572/0.422 (events -0035, -0014, -0042, -0049). ## H3 — quench/post-heat residence
**Unresolved. Pre-test prediction:** A replicate 390 K/1800 s followed by immediate quench should resemble direct termination if termination already freezes chemistry. An otherwise matched 1800 s unstirred/stirred wait without quench may continue conversion during cooling; if conversion/yield or degradation rises beyond assay/process uncertainty, termination timing matters. If both agree with direct termination, H3 will be rejected in this scope.

# Hypothesis notebook

## H2 — catalyst identity

**Supported in tested catalyst-B/water scope:** Conversion and yield rose strongly with actual temperature and residence time, but prolonged/high exposure increased byproduct and degradation and lowered selectivity. Relevant final assays: 330/1800 (-0035), 360/1800 (-0014), 390/600 (-0056), 390/1800 (-0042), 390/3600 (-0063), 420/1800 (-0049). Repeat 390 K/1800 s, quench, then wait 1800 s. # Hypothesis notebook — final source-stage synthesis

## H2 — catalyst identity
**Supported within one matched screen:** In water at a 360 K target for 1800 s, Catalyst B produced the best final-assay yield/selectivity among A–D (events runner-operation-0007, -0014, -0021, -0028). The close match in actual temperature increments excludes thermal mismatch as the main explanation. Scope is limited by lack of replicated identity screens and no solvent variation.

## H1 — temperature/time network
**Supported:** With catalyst B/water, conversion and target yield increase with actual thermal exposure across the tested temperature and time series (events -0035, -0014, -0042, -0049 and -0056, -0042, -0063). However, prolonged exposure increases byproduct/degradation and lowers selectivity: at 390 K, extending from 1800 to 3600 s raised final yield ~0.317→0.453 but degradation warning ~0.014→0.066 and selectivity ~0.716→0.671. A minimal explanatory account is parallel target/byproduct formation plus an exposure-dependent secondary loss or degradation channel. The data do not uniquely distinguish direct reactant-to-degradation from target-to-degradation.

## H3 — post-heat chemistry and quench
**Strongly supported:** An unquenched 1800 s wait after 390 K/1800 s heating cooled the vessel by ~44 K but increased final conversion/yield to ~0.618/~0.418 and degradation warning to ~0.052 (event -0079), versus direct termination ~0.417/~0.317 and ~0.014 (event -0042).

Thus quench arrests the reactive network in this scope rather than merely providing equivalent passive cooling.

## Predictive scope and operating decision
Predictions should use actual temperature/time history, including cooling residence and quench state, not nominal heater duration alone. Higher exposure raises conversion but eventually sacrifices selectivity and degradation performance. Batch 11 offers a favorable observed compromise: 390 K target for 1800 s followed by 1800 s unquenched cooling residence, then termination, with final yield ~0.418, score ~0.239, and safety risk ~0.128. Batch 9 gives higher yield (~0.453) but more degradation and a lower score. This recommendation would change if priority shifted to maximum yield regardless of degradation, or if replication showed the batch-11 advantage was not reproducible.

# Mechanistic report

## 1. Scope and evidential basis

This report describes the anonymous benchmark reaction system explored in 12 completed batches. It is a phenomenological kinetic account, not a molecular-structure assignment. The catalyst identities and reaction species were deliberately anonymous, so terms such as reactant, target, byproduct, and degradation product refer to observable roles rather than named compounds.

Every batch used 0.040 mol limiting reagent, 0.005 mol catalyst, 0.080 L water, and 500 rpm stirring during commanded heating. Consequently, the conclusions apply most directly to this composition and mixing regime. Final-assay results are the primary basis for comparisons between completed batches; intermediate HPLC measurements were useful corroboration but were not treated as exact replicates of the final assay.

## 2. Proposed process network

The smallest model consistent with the observations is a temperature-dependent, catalyst-modulated network containing productive conversion, competing conversion, and exposure-dependent degradation:

R --kP(T,C)--> P
R --kB(T,C)--> B
P --kD(T,C)--> D

Here R is the limiting reactant, P the desired target, B a competing byproduct pool, D a degradation or secondary-product pool, and C denotes catalyst identity and active fraction.

A useful working set of equations is:

- dR/dt = -a(t)[kP(T,C) + kB(T,C)]R
- dP/dt = a(t)kP(T,C)R - kD(T,C)P
- dB/dt = a(t)kB(T,C)R + alpha·kD(T,C)P
- da/dt = -kdeact(T,C)a

The available data do not require catalyst deactivation, so the last equation remains optional. Depletion of R plus increasing secondary degradation can already generate the observed decline in selectivity at long exposure. A direct R-to-D branch is another observationally equivalent possibility.

The rate constants plausibly obey Arrhenius-like temperature dependence,

k_i(T,C) = A_i(C) exp[-E_i(C)/(RT)],

but the campaign did not provide enough independent temperature/time combinations to identify numerical activation energies or pre-exponential factors. Catalyst identity appears to alter both total activity and the branching ratio kP/kB, not merely multiply all rates by the same factor.

Temperature must be treated as a trajectory rather than a nominal label. A conceptual thermal equation is

dT/dt = (Tset - T)/tau_heat
under active heating, followed by passive cooling after heater removal. Reaction continues during that cooling trajectory unless the batch is quenched. In pseudocode:

for each short interval dt:
    update actual T from heating or cooling dynamics
    if not quenched:
        update R, P, B, D using temperature-dependent rates
    else:
        set effective reaction rates approximately to zero

This last quench rule is strongly supported by the dedicated termination experiments.

## 3. Catalyst identity controls productive branching

Batches 1–4 formed a matched catalyst screen at a 360 K target for 1800 s. Their reported heat-induced temperature increments were all approximately 60.10 K, so gross thermal mismatch is not a satisfactory explanation for the differences.

Final-assay observations were:

- Batch 1, Catalyst A: conversion 0.2830, yield 0.1300, selectivity 0.4480, byproduct 0.1519, degradation warning 0.0000.
- Batch 2, Catalyst B: conversion 0.2757, yield 0.1996, selectivity 0.7237, byproduct 0.0848, degradation warning 0.0111.
- Batch 3, Catalyst C: conversion 0.2262, yield 0.1354, selectivity 0.5502, byproduct 0.1116, degradation warning 0.0096.
- Batch 4, Catalyst D: conversion 0.2725, yield 0.1637, selectivity 0.6871, byproduct 0.0925, degradation warning 0.0034.

Catalyst B did not merely maximize conversion: its conversion was similar to A and D, but it delivered much higher target selectivity than A and higher final yield than all alternatives. This supports a catalyst-dependent branching ratio. In the model, Catalyst B has a more favorable kP/kB ratio under these conditions. Catalyst D may also have a favorable branch ratio, though its final yield was lower.

One caution is the discrepancy in Batch 4: HPLC measured yield about 0.1992 before termination, whereas the final assay reported about 0.1637. This difference is larger than the nominal measurement noise and could reflect sampling heterogeneity, assay-specific process uncertainty, or genuine change between measurements. It limits precise ranking of B versus D, but it does not erase the broad conclusion that A was substantially less selective and B was the best observed catalyst overall. The catalyst screen had no independent replication, so catalyst-by-temperature interactions remain unidentified.

## 4. Temperature accelerates both target formation and competing chemistry

For Catalyst B at 1800 s, Batches 5, 2, 6, and 7 varied the target temperature from 330 to 420 K. The reported heat-induced temperature increments were approximately 30.95, 60.11, 89.26, and 118.41 K, respectively. Final-assay results were:

- Batch 5, 330 K: conversion 0.1666, yield 0.0995, selectivity 0.6516, byproduct 0.0664, degradation 0.0000, safety risk 0.0884.
- Batch 2, 360 K: conversion 0.2757, yield 0.1996, selectivity 0.7237, byproduct 0.0848, degradation 0.0111, safety risk 0.1077.
- Batch 6, 390 K: conversion 0.4172, yield 0.3167, selectivity 0.7165, byproduct 0.1171, degradation 0.0141, safety risk 0.1757.
- Batch 7, 420 K: conversion 0.5722, yield 0.4218, selectivity 0.7275, byproduct 0.1598, degradation 0.0153, safety risk 0.3419.

Conversion and yield increased strongly with temperature. This is consistent with thermally activated kinetics rather than a temperature-independent clock. Byproduct signal also increased, showing that the competing channel accelerates as well. Selectivity was low at 330 K, improved by 360 K, and remained near 0.72 through 420 K. Therefore, within 330–420 K and at 1800 s, the productive and competing channels have broadly similar high-temperature acceleration, although the low-temperature selectivity result suggests their activation responses are not exactly identical.

The safety response was much more nonlinear: Batch 7 reached risk 0.3419, narrowly below the published 0.35 limit. Thus 420 K gave the largest 1800 s yield but very little safety margin. This is an observed operational boundary, not evidence of a chemical discontinuity at 0.35.

## 5. Residence time reveals secondary competition or degradation

At a 390 K target with Catalyst B, Batches 8, 6, and 9 varied commanded hot residence time:

- Batch 8, 600 s: conversion 0.1328, yield 0.1072, selectivity 0.7416, byproduct 0.0369, degradation 0.0000.
- Batch 6, 1800 s: conversion 0.4172, yield 0.3167, selectivity 0.7165, byproduct 0.1171, degradation 0.0141.
- Batch 9, 3600 s: conversion 0.6764, yield 0.4530, selectivity 0.6714, byproduct 0.2304, degradation 0.0656.

Longer residence increased conversion and absolute target yield, but selectivity declined from about 0.742 to 0.671 and degradation warning increased from zero to about 0.066. Byproduct rose more rapidly than target yield at long time. This caused me to reject a simple one-channel model in which R converts only to stable P. A parallel byproduct channel is necessary, and either target degradation, catalyst selectivity drift, or a late-stage reactant-to-degradation pathway is additionally plausible.

The data do not identify which late-stage mechanism dominates:

1. P may be converted into D or B after formation.
2. R may feed a separate degradation channel that becomes important at high conversion.
3. Catalyst B may deactivate selectively, suppressing productive conversion more strongly than competing conversion.
4. Accumulating products may alter effective rate constants or inhibit the productive pathway.

All four can produce increasing conversion accompanied by falling selectivity. Time-resolved species measurements within the same vessel would be required to distinguish them.

## 6. Chemistry continues during passive cooling

A major revision to the initial explanation came from Batch 11. It received the same 390 K/1800 s heating program as Batch 6, followed by an unquenched 1800 s wait. During that wait the reported temperature fell by about 44.31 K, but substantial chemistry continued.

Comparison of final assays:

- Batch 6, direct termination: conversion 0.4172, yield 0.3167, selectivity 0.7165, byproduct 0.1171, degradation 0.0141.
- Batch 11, 1800 s unquenched wait: conversion 0.6185, yield 0.4178, selectivity 0.6719, byproduct 0.1988, degradation 0.0523.

Thus heater shutdown did not terminate the network. During cooling residence, conversion rose by roughly 0.20 and yield by roughly 0.10, while selectivity deteriorated and degradation increased. Nominal heater-on time alone is therefore not predictive. The important exposure variable is an integral over actual temperature history, schematically

Omega_i = integral k_i[T(t),C] dt,

including the cooling period.

Batch 11 also shows that meaningful reaction rates persist well below the peak temperature. Because temperature and elapsed cooling time changed together, the experiment does not locate the precise temperature window responsible for this conversion.

## 7. Quench arrests the network rather than merely cooling it

Batches 10 and 12 tested quenching after the standard 390 K/1800 s treatment. The quench cooled the vessel by 45 K in about 55 s.

- Batch 10, immediate quench then termination: conversion 0.4183, yield 0.2930, selectivity 0.7174, byproduct 0.1194, degradation 0.0107.
- Batch 12, quench then 1800 s wait: conversion 0.4272, yield 0.3065, selectivity 0.7214, byproduct 0.1086, degradation 0.0156.
- Batch 11, no quench then 1800 s wait: conversion 0.6185, yield 0.4178, selectivity 0.6719, byproduct 0.1988, degradation 0.0523.

The decisive comparison is Batch 12 versus Batch 11. Both included an 1800 s post-heating wait, but only Batch 12 was quenched first. Batch 12 remained near the immediate-quench/direct-termination region, whereas Batch 11 underwent extensive additional conversion and degradation. Therefore, quenching changes more than the thermal trajectory: operationally, it suppresses the reactive network to nearly zero on the timescale tested.

The small differences between Batches 10 and 12 are compatible with run variation and assay uncertainty, although they do not prove that every microscopic reaction rate is exactly zero after quench. The strong conclusion is that any residual post-quench change is far smaller than unquenched cooling chemistry.

## 8. Interpretation of conversion, selectivity, and yield

Across most batches, yield approximately tracks conversion multiplied by selectivity, supporting the interpretation that selectivity represents the fraction of converted material associated with target formation. The equality is not exact in every assay, so these observables should be modeled jointly rather than forcing an algebraic identity without an error term.

A useful observation model would be:

observed conversion = 1 - R/R0 + measurement error
observed yield = P/Pmax + measurement error
observed selectivity approximately equals yield/conversion + measurement/process error
byproduct signal = scaled function of B and possibly D
degradation warning = scaled function of D

The scale factors are not identified. In particular, byproduct signal and degradation warning should not be interpreted as molar concentrations without calibration information.

## 9. Operational prediction within the explored region

Within the tested composition, I expect the following qualitative behavior:

- Increasing actual thermal exposure will initially raise conversion and target yield.
- At longer exposure, byproduct and degradation will grow and selectivity will decline.
- Catalyst B will usually outperform A and C in target selectivity near the tested 360–390 K range; superiority over D is probable but less firmly resolved.
- An unquenched cooling residence after heating will continue both productive and competing conversion.
- A quench immediately after the desired exposure will largely freeze conversion, selectivity, and degradation state.
- Extrapolating above 420 K is unsafe and scientifically unsupported; even 420 K/1800 s approached the safety limit.

Batch 11 was the selected operating recommendation because it gave the highest observed campaign score, approximately 0.2394, with yield 0.4178 and final reported safety risk 0.1279. Its process was a 390 K target for 1800 s followed by 1800 s unquenched cooling residence and termination. This was a compromise rather than a maximum-yield condition. Batch 9 produced higher yield, 0.4530, but had lower selectivity, higher degradation warning, and a lower score of approximately 0.2283.

If the sole objective were maximum observed yield regardless of degradation, Batch 9 would be preferred. If preservation of selectivity and low degradation were dominant, the 1800 s 390 K treatment followed by prompt quench would be preferable. These distinctions demonstrate that “best condition” is objective-dependent.

## 10. Limits, unidentified factors, and competing explanations

The principal limitations are:

- Only water was tested. Solvent effects and solvent–catalyst interactions are completely unidentified.
- Reagent amount, catalyst loading, concentration, and stirring rate were fixed. No kinetic order can be inferred.
- Catalyst identity was screened at only one temperature and time, without replication. Catalyst rankings may change elsewhere.
- Temperature was represented by operation-level trajectory summaries rather than a dense time series. Numerical activation parameters cannot be estimated reliably.
- Pressure, atmosphere, headspace, and feedback-control settings were not varied.
- The anonymous observation channels do not establish molecular identities or elementary steps.
- HPLC and final assays occasionally differed beyond their nominal analytical noise, indicating process or sampling variation that cannot be separated with the available design.
- Byproduct and degradation observables may overlap chemically; the data only justify treating them as distinct reported channels.

Reasonable competing models include parallel R-to-P and R-to-B conversion without P degradation, but with catalyst deactivation or changing selectivity; reversible target formation followed by trapping during quench; product inhibition; or multiple unobserved catalyst states. The present network is preferred because it is the simplest account of rising conversion, declining long-time selectivity, increasing degradation warning, continued cooling-phase chemistry, and quench arrest. It should not be mistaken for a uniquely identified elementary mechanism.
